title: How Board Breaking Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss board breaking (tameshiwari) in martial arts. They open by explaining the swap from a planned Mars episode, then cover the Indonesian pencak silat origin legend (Rama Sukana and the monkey), karate's origins in weapon bans on the peasantry, and the strength of bone and how knockouts happen from head spin. They explain how boards are typically broken (pine, about a foot wide, three-quarters inch thick, struck in the center with palm heel, hammer fist or knife hand, going with the grain), why you must follow through and not pull the punch, and the physics of velocity, mass and force, including physicist and astronaut Ronald McNair's research and his karate uniform at Kennedy Space Center. They discuss breaking-board records, the UFC downward elbow strike rule legend, and close with listener mail about a pin setter's experiences in 1960s Cleveland.

segments.title: Episode swap and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck explain they swapped a planned Mars episode for board breaking, which they had not covered before. They give an early safety warning not to break boards without training, and note glass, ice and concrete are also broken.

segments.title: Origins of board breaking and the monkey legend
segments.summary: They discuss tameshiwari, the Japanese term for board breaking, and distinguish staged 'physics assisted' breaks from real ones. They tell the legend of Rama Sukana from Bawean, who learned monkey fighting by a river and defeated her husband. They contrast pencak silat with karate and note the cobra kai name.

segments.title: Karate's roots and the history of breaking boards
segments.summary: They say karate means empty hand and that it may have developed when the Japanese feudal government stripped peasants of weapons in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. The hosts say they could not find where board breaking originated, only customary wood choices such as cedar.

segments.title: Bone strength, the instinct to pull back, and knockouts
segments.summary: They discuss how strong bone is, comparing it to pickup trucks and concrete, with the caveat that speed and delivery matter. They describe knockouts from head spin, the brain shutting down at high rotation, and the force a boxer generates, about five thousand newtons.

segments.title: How boards are set up and struck
segments.summary: They describe typical boards: about a foot wide, roughly three-quarters inch thick, usually pine rather than hardwood. Strikes are aimed at the center, using palm heel, hammer fist or knife hand. Breaking with the grain is easier. They mention the Karate Kid ice scene and say they have not seen a board broken in person.

segments.title: Focus, breathing, follow-through and physics of force
segments.summary: They explain that focus and breathing (kiai) help avoid pulling the punch, which can cause injury as force rebounds. The peak of a strike occurs before contact, so follow-through matters. Velocity and mass produce force, and they discuss the physicist and astronaut Ronald McNair, whose karate uniform is displayed at Kennedy Space Center.

segments.title: Listener mail: pin setter and closing remarks
segments.summary: Closing discussion covers the Ronald McNair research, stacked boards, board breaking records, and the UFC downward elbow strike rule legend. The hosts end with listener mail from Ray Hovorka about his father's job as a pin setter in 1960s Cleveland.
